name: Trap Botox (Barbie Botox)

lead: Trap Botox, popularly called Barbie Botox, is botulinum toxin injected into the trapezius so the neck looks longer and the slope from neck to shoulder looks softer and slimmer. It went viral under the Barbie Botox name.

The toxin weakens the injected muscle so it relaxes and loses bulk over time, changing the shoulder-neck line. A 2024 systematic review in the Journal of Plastic, Reconstructive & Aesthetic Surgery examined the trend, and trapezius injection is also used in clinical settings such as chronic migraine and cervical dystonia. Detailed cosmetic outcome data for this look are limited.

paras: A clinician injects the trapezius in an office visit, and people repeat treatments as the effect wears off over months. Results build gradually as the muscle relaxes, and it is sometimes mentioned alongside other toxin treatments.
It is an off-label cosmetic use of a prescription product. Neck and shoulder muscle weakness is a general toxin concern, and the effect is temporary.

angle.text: Trap Botox is promoted to relax the trapezius so the neck looks longer and the shoulder line more slender. The toxin weakens the muscle so it loses bulk over time. It is an off-label cosmetic use; a 2024 systematic review covers the trend.

lead: Trap Botox, popularly called "Barbie Botox", is the injection of botulinum toxin into the trapezius muscle, the slope of muscle between neck and shoulder. People seek it to relax and slim the muscle so the neck looks longer and more slender and the shoulder line looks narrower and more sloped.[1][1]

It is an off-label cosmetic use of a toxin that is approved for other purposes: Botox Cosmetic was approved by the FDA in 2002 for frown lines, and botulinum toxin is also used for conditions such as cervical dystonia and chronic migraine, where injections go into neck and shoulder muscles.[2][3][4] Wikipedia's botulinum toxin article does not mention trapezius injections for appearance.[2]

A 2024 letter in the Journal of Plastic, Reconstructive & Aesthetic Surgery titled "Barbie botox": The systematic review of a popular trend comments on three published articles on botulinum toxin for trapezius hypertrophy. The record is listed as a comment and letter and carries no abstract.[1]

paras: The procedure aims to reduce trapezius bulk using a neuromodulator so the neck-shoulder line looks elongated.[1] Botulinum toxin weakens the injected muscle; for facial cosmetic uses the smoothing is usually visible three to five days after injection, peaks about a week later and typically lasts two to four months, after which muscles can be retreated.[2] Trapezius duration is not described in the sources reviewed.

sections.h: Medical use of neck and trapezius injections
paras: Botulinum toxin is used for cervical dystonia and for chronic migraine, which the FDA approved in 2010; injection sites for these include neck and shoulder muscles.[2] Registered trials of toxin in neck muscles, such as an injection-site study in cervical dystonia that lists the trapezius among seven muscle groups, address medical conditions rather than appearance.[3][4] Another registered trial studied toxin for neck contractures after radiosurgery.[5]

For botulinum toxin in general, Wikipedia lists unintended muscle weakness, difficulty swallowing, headaches, flu-like symptoms and allergic reactions, and notes that the toxin can spread from the injection site; the FDA added boxed warnings about spread in 2009.[2] Repeated high doses can cause muscle atrophy or weakness, which reportedly recovers after a break.[2] Specific adverse-event data for cosmetic trapezius injection were not found.

No studies found of trapezius toxin for cosmetic neck appearance beyond published commentary on trapezius hypertrophy treatment.[1] Registered trials involving trapezius injection address cervical dystonia and migraine.[3][4]

timeline.event: FDA approves Botox Cosmetic for frown lines.[2]
Botulinum toxin is FDA-approved for chronic migraine.[2]
JPRAS publishes a letter on "Barbie botox" and trapezius hypertrophy.[1]
